nodes.summary: A group $G$ is $p$-soluble when it has a chain of subgroups $1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \cdots \le H_n = G$, each normal in the next, such that for every $i < n$ the relative index $|H_{i+1} : H_i|$ (taken to be $0$ when it is infinite) is a power of $p$ or is coprime to $p$. For a finite group this says that every factor $H_{i+1}/H_i$ is a $p$-group or a $p'$-group.

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a prime, $G$ a finite group whose order is divisible by $p$, and $P$ a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$. If every maximal subgroup $M$ of $P$ has a $p$-soluble supplement in $G$, that is, a $p$-soluble subgroup $K$ of $G$ with $MK = G$, then $G$ is $p$-soluble.
